title: Fine-Tuning at Home: Beat Frontier Models With 8 Steps
description: A two-host walkthrough of a knowledge graph built from Maxime Rivest's article "Even you can now fine-tune an LLM, and maybe you finally should." The claim: with a coding agent, a frontier "teacher" model and LoRA adapters on consumer hardware, fine-tuning a task-specific model is now something one person can do. Covers the eight-step workflow, synthetic distillation, why training loss kept improving while rubric scores plateaued, the roughly 1,000-example saturation point, the break-even math (about 170 papers per hour), licensing limits on training with model outputs, and the last-mile accuracy problem. Benchmark figures are the author's own reported results.

title: Super Is Not Superior
description: A deep dive into Tejas Kumar's essay "AI Is Now SI: Super Intelligence Isn't Superior," via a knowledge graph of its argument. The essay says "super" describes task performance while "superior" claims worth, and that renaming AI "Super Intelligence" blurs the two. Covers Bostrom's definition of superintelligence, real machine milestones, the BCG "jagged frontier" study, the golden calf, Calvin's "forge of idols," the sun renamed "the greater light" in Genesis, and the essay's case for loyalty as a willingness to overpay. 2026 events are as reported in the essay.

title: When Your GTM Brain Lives in Git
description: A two-host walkthrough of a knowledge graph built from John Kutay's post "GTM in git," based on his San Francisco talk "Your GTM Belongs in git." The argument: put as much go-to-market work as possible into a git repo that coding agents can reason over, test and scale, with the repo as the "logical brain" and hosted infrastructure taking over only when scale demands it. Covers Rippling's GrowthOS (usage figures are self-reported), agent harnesses and sandboxes, GTM evals, context engineering and shared definitions, and the marketer-as-AI-engineer shift. Also the graph's own additions: a GitOps lineage, a governance caution about agents querying production data, and why "ideas become the bottleneck" is still a contested prediction.

title: The Slop Superhighway
description: Rhys Sullivan argues that agents flooding human channels like GitHub issues isn't the real failure. The failure is that there's no agent-to-agent channel to carry that traffic, so humans end up as 'meat proxies' copy-pasting between AIs. We walk through his first-person Cloudflare bug story (single-sourced), the 2025 issueslop backlash, what exists today (author-side issue triage, MCP, A2A), and what's still missing: identity, payments, and defenses against prompt injection. We close with economics and liability lenses, which the knowledge graph adds as its own speculative extensions rather than claims from the post.

title: How to Research Anything
description: A walk through Polymath Investor's practitioner guide to independent research: scope a small question that passes the 'So what?' test, cap your time, skim twenty sources and read three deeply, check key facts against three independent witnesses, and decide what 'done' means before you start. The knowledge graph adds its own theory lenses, flagged as interpretation, most notably that the guide's 'plateau of diminishing returns' mirrors the foraging rule ecologists use for when an animal should move on. We also cover the tensions the graph raises and the guide leaves unaddressed: AI summaries may erode the outsider's fresh eyes, and expert calls aren't independent witnesses. The guide is one person's advice, not a tested method, and its paywalled section is known only from a teaser.

title: How to Research Anything, Part 1: The Method
description: Part 1 of a two-parter on Polymath Investor's practitioner guide to independent research. We walk one made-up project through the whole method: scope a small question that passes the 'So what?' test, cap your time, choose sources that will still matter in a year, skim twenty and read three deeply, check key facts against three independent witnesses, keep one-idea notes with their sources, and decide what 'done' means before you start. The guide is one person's untested advice, and its paywalled section is known only from a teaser. Ends with a teaser for Part 2.

title: How to Research Anything, Part 2: Why It Works
description: Part 2 opens with a quick recap of the method, then looks at why it might work and where it falls short. The knowledge graph adds outside theories, all flagged as interpretation: the guide's 'plateau of diminishing returns' mirrors ecology's rule for when a forager should leave a patch, 'useful a year from now?' estimates how fast a field's facts go stale, and a pre-set 'done' is Herbert Simon's satisficing. Then two tensions the guide leaves unaddressed: AI summaries may erode the outsider's fresh eyes, and expert calls aren't independent witnesses. We close with cross-domain synthesis and the author's compounding research playbook.

title: Cancer's Second Verb: Converting Tumors Instead of Killing Them
description: A walk through a knowledge graph built from Brian Roemmele's X post on a KAIST study (Advanced Science, 2024). As the post tells it, researchers built a 'digital twin' of an intestinal cell's gene network, used an algorithm called BENEIN to pick three genes (MYB, HDAC2, FOXA2), and turned colon cancer cells into normal-like cells in cell lines and mice by maturing them rather than killing them. This is early preclinical work with no human data, described secondhand, and nothing here is medical advice. The graph adds context: differentiation therapy has treated the leukemia APL for decades, the idea builds on Waddington, Kauffman and Yamanaka, and hard-to-drug targets, durability (speculative) and the tumor's surroundings could keep it from becoming a therapy.

title: Prediction Markets, Part 1: How a Price Becomes a Forecast
description: Part 1 of a two-parter built from a knowledge graph on prediction markets. A contract pays one dollar if an event happens, so its price reads as a probability. We cover why economists think that should work (Hayek's idea that prices pool scattered knowledge, plus Arrow-Debreu and efficient markets), the automated market maker that keeps thin markets trading, corporate markets at firms like Google, and how the law shaped the field: Iowa Electronic Markets, Intrade's shutdown, Polymarket's exit and 2025 return, and Kalshi's court win. We end with catastrophe bonds as an older, professional version of the same idea. Dated events were checked against news coverage. Not betting or investment advice.

title: Prediction Markets, Part 2: When the Price Lies
description: Part 2 opens with a quick recap, then a March 2025 Polymarket market on a Ukraine minerals deal that, per news reports, resolved 'yes' with no deal signed after a token-holder vote. We cover the favorite-longshot bias (prices act like betting odds in the tails), wash trading and why volume isn't proof (estimates vary widely), oracles as the real point of centralization, and the parallel with catastrophe-bond triggers. Then the rivals: the Good Judgment Project's superforecasters and no-money platforms like Metaculus and Manifold, where the comparisons are messy. We close with futarchy, Hanson's untested idea to 'vote on values, bet on beliefs.' Not betting or investment advice.

title: References, Part 1: The Police Sketch
description: How Brett Berson's composite referencing works: references as a police sketch built from many witnesses, front-door and back-door calls, the whose-side-are-they-on check, story-and-comparison questions, the 12/5/3 call counts, running references early because of confirmation bias, and how to judge the person giving the reference.

title: References, Part 2: Marriage After a Second Date
description: Why Berson's reference method works and where it falls short: hiring as marriage after a second date, context-dependent performance, the hardwired-traits debate and selection research, legal limits on what references say, AI-summarized reference calls, two-way due diligence, and the method's roots in Graham Duncan's essay.

title: Spotting Weakness in Seconds: Prison Eyes and Miami Doors
description: A deep dive into a viral post claiming inmates can spot a 'weak man' in seconds: the 1981 and 2013 victim-selection studies behind it, thin-slicing and psychopathy, the leap to Miami's velvet ropes and the walled-garden roots of 'paradise', and how the post's wolves-and-sheep rhetoric doubles as its paywall pitch.

title: Hiring in the Age of AI, Part 1: What Survived the Interview Lab
description: JD Pruett's 20/10 philosophy: when coding agents eat the middle 70% of a project, hire for the first 20% (framing, architecture, taste) and the last 10% (shipping). We walk through the interview formats he tried and dropped — the agent-assisted long onsite, the AI systems design round, rule-of-thumb trivia — and the two that survived: unassisted code review with 'what if' changes, and an onsite that opens with a market presentation and then three shrinking timed problems, all judged by whether interviewers can give a confident thumbs up or down.

title: Hiring in the Age of AI, Part 2: Judging Depth You Can't Check
description: How do you judge a candidate whose field you don't know? Pruett's rules of thumb: deep versus shallow simplicity, speed under pressure, a walk-through of a problem from 18+ months ago, and telling people who recognize the underlying problem from people who match on surface labels — backed by the 1981 Chi, Feltovich and Glaser physics-sorting study, and the idea that agent 'memory' is really cache invalidation. Then the pushback: trading standardization for interviewer confidence, and a speculative worry about where junior engineers get their reps.

title: The New Manager, Part 1: You Are the Weather
description: Louise Deason's 'Ten things nobody tells you when you become a manager', things one to five: your output is the team's output, stop doing the work and hand over outcomes, touch nothing for the first few weeks, you are the weather, and let your reports run the one-on-one. Plus context the source map adds, not Deason: the Peter Principle, the Theory of Constraints, Chesterton's fence, and why a leader's idle remark lands as an order.

title: The New Manager, Part 2: The Seat You Took
description: Things six to ten from Louise Deason's essay: absorb the mess from above and argue it upstairs, manage your own manager, give hard feedback early and kindly, keep receipts so you can fight for people in rooms they're not in, and know that management is no longer a safe seat. Plus the source map's own additions: emotional labor, psychological safety, the 'unbossing' squeeze on middle managers (including a reported Gartner forecast), and the algorithmic boss.

title: The New CFO, Part 1: From Scorekeeper to Builder
description: Seema Amble's a16z essay argues AI is rewriting the CFO job: from producing numbers to designing the company's operating system. We cover the four CFO eras, how cheap data turns the finance stack into a teammate, skills maintained like code, the zero-day close, agents and compute on the P&L, and why controls are what make speed safe. Company examples are attributed, not verified.

title: The New CFO, Part 2: The Finance Engineer
description: The people side of Seema Amble's 'You Need a New CFO': the finance engineer, vibecoding, teams shrinking from about 5% of headcount toward 2%, why senior experts like the head of tax gain most from AI, and 'walk me through your prompt sequence.' Plus three ideas the knowledge map adds on top of the essay, including a speculative worry about the career ladder.

title: The Software Foreman, Part 1: Attention, Not Code
description: Stephen Margheim argues AI in software is optimizing the wrong thing: his team's bottleneck isn't writing code, it's attention. We cover the software factory vs the software foreman, a bug that broke links only for unused accounts and was found by luck, Claude debugging it from a single message link, and the data lake and query-based watches that give attention a place to look.

title: The Software Foreman, Part 2: Watch Everything, Interrupt Rarely
description: How Margheim's software foreman thinks: notice, hypothesize, check, then drop it or escalate with evidence. Plus persistent background agents, his 'noise beats silence' stance, the crying-wolf risk, and the ten-minute human review. Then four ideas the knowledge map adds on its own: control charts, Toyota's gemba walk, Herbert Simon on attention, and the METR study where developers felt faster but were slower.

title: The Night AI Emptied Math's Open Problems, Part 1: Scooped
description: A Proofs and Prompts post collects 100+ mathematicians' reactions to OpenAI's reported October 6 release of hundreds of claimed solutions to open problems. Part 1 covers the event, proofs arriving faster than anyone can read them, withdrawals and partial formal checks, Peter Scholze's cryptography worry, a declined advisory recommendation, and three hard-hit voices: Wilton, Zaremsky and Duminil-Copin. Counts and verification status are as reported in the post, not independently confirmed.

title: The Night AI Emptied Math's Open Problems, Part 2: Grieving and Thrilled
description: The human side of mathematicians' reactions to the AI math release: PhD students and postdocs facing scooped theses, Tasmin Chu's grant and security worries, Cyril Houdayer's genuine thrill, Terence Tao on losing the first encounter with a problem, the unpaid work of reading and explaining the proofs, Danny Calegari's zippers, and a thread of Dolly Parton, Solaris and E. E. Cummings.

title: The AI Value Creation Problem, Part 1: Two of Three Levers
description: Mark Ajzenstadt argues private equity AI plans collapse into headcount cuts because they fit the earnings bridge, while returns come from three levers: earnings growth, the exit multiple and time. We walk through his illustrative math where one point of multiple erases 60% of the equity gain, Bain's tougher return arithmetic, and the diligence question he expects next. The author discloses a commercial interest; cited reports are as summarized in his essay.

title: The AI Value Creation Problem, Part 2: Proprietary Observation
description: Why the people a payroll spreadsheet marks as savings may hold a company's real AI advantage: Box and Ramp data on AI leaders growing headcount, Gartner's rehiring forecast, 'proprietary observation beats proprietary data,' fieldwork, release quality, a vendor case study we treat as illustration only, and portfolio reuse, plus a fund-fee incentive the knowledge map adds.

title: How Stories Create Alignment, Part 1: The Story as Operating System
description: Hiten Shah argues a company runs on one shared story: held in the same words by every team, owned and retold by the founder, and used as a yes-or-no filter for decisions. We cover his five ideas, then the research the knowledge map adds (not cited by Shah) to explain why it might work: Fisher's narrative paradigm, narrative transportation and neural coupling, shared mental models, Weick, Schein and Rumelt.

title: How Stories Create Alignment, Part 2: When the Story Goes Wrong
description: Beyond Hiten Shah's essay, entirely the knowledge map's additions: Shiller's narrative economics, category design and stories as replicators, then two failure modes Shah doesn't address, narrative lock-in and the map's own speculative idea of 'narrative debt', plus speculative takes on the story as lossy compression and AI agents that retell or counterfeit a founder's story.

title: Mining the Sky, Part 1: The Jar and the Asteroid
description: Devon Eriksen's viral post, replying to Elon Musk, argues Earth's valuable metals sank to the core and the ones we mine came from asteroids. We unpack his jar thought experiment and the real science under it (planetary differentiation, Goldschmidt's element classes, the late veneer), then the knowledge map's main pushback: 'every mine is an asteroid strike' is right about where the atoms came from but mostly wrong about how ore deposits form. Plus why the post's combative tone matters.

title: Mining the Sky, Part 2: Rockets, Railroads and Real Estate
description: The economics of Devon Eriksen's off-world industry vision: the rocket equation as the real snag, making things in space, self-replicating factories (speculative), SpaceX's launch dominance and the railroad analogy, orbital solar versus cheap Earth solar, fusion's actual status, who can own an asteroid, Gerard O'Neill's 1976 High Frontier, and the space-junk problem the post never mentions.

title: Too Many Interests, Part 1: The System
description: Dan Koe argues that having many interests is an asset: one transformation, Point A to Point B, ties them into a single brand, planned on a paper content map. Attract broadly, monetize narrowly, and you only need to be one step ahead. We flag the map's own additions: Herbert Simon's attention economics, a speculative link to Scott Adams' talent stack, and its reading of Koe's school story. Source: Koe's X article 'Full Course: How To Turn Your Interests Into a Profitable Lifestyle Business,' via an IntuiBloom knowledge graph. Koe promotes his own platform, Eden.

title: Too Many Interests, Part 2: The Money and the Risk Nobody Names
description: Koe's money machine: a $19 micro product, a $500-$1000 four-call service, angle mining, an application form that replaces the sales page, a four-step DM ladder, and AI that reprices common know-how. Then Eden, Koe's own platform, 'soft rich' economics, and the map's critique: a single point of failure across one social platform, one vendor and one AI provider. Prices and income figures are Koe's claims, not verified.

title: Models as Insiders, Part 1: The Insider Frame
description: Satya Nadella argues frontier AI models should be governed as privileged insiders: not because they are malicious, but because anything that capable with that much access can err or be compromised. We cover his split between the supply of intelligence and authority over it, containment-first engineering, and his seven observability principles. Then we flag the map's own background additions: insider threat programs, Saltzer and Schroeder, Ken Thompson's Trusting Trust, and the principal-agent problem. Source: Nadella's X article 'Models as Insider Risks in the Super Intelligence Era,' via an IntuiBloom knowledge graph.

title: Models as Insiders, Part 2: Who Watches the Watcher
description: What if the thing checking an AI model is another black box? Nadella's nested-black-box warning, his call for chain-of-thought transparency, and his model-diversity rule, set against the map's counterweights: research showing explanations aren't always faithful, the 1986 Knight and Leveson experiment where independent software versions failed together, AI control research, interpretability, the ironies of automation, and the standards and liability layers where containment gets enforced.

title: Code Lies, Facts Don't, Part 1: Three Bugs
description: Cindy Sridharan argues code is an unreliable narrator: it tells you what can happen, not what did. Three real bugs she debugged with an AI agent: a latency spike where a plausible certificate theory passed review but was wrong, and the real clue was 5 versus 400 DNS addresses; a memory leak that took three wrong answers and turned out to have two causes; and a hang found four layers down, in one line of a 30 MB kernel dump. Source: her Medium essay 'How to effectively debug when you no longer understand the code,' via an IntuiBloom knowledge graph.

title: Code Lies, Facts Don't, Part 2: The Method
description: Sridharan's method for debugging code you can't read: facts as fixed constraints and hypotheses that must satisfy every one, controls and 'sad paths', a hypotheses-by-fact table that ranks clues, five tactics for repairing broken theories, and descending layers for new signals. Why AI-made repros and same-model reviews are weaker safeguards than they look, why demanding citations works, and her 'agent-native software factory' that counts every human intervention as a gap.

title: Stop Reading the Code, Part 1: Signals, Not Stories
description: A second, exploratory map of Cindy Sridharan's essay 'How to effectively debug when you no longer understand the code' reaches beyond her method. We recap her debugging loop, then follow the map outward: why dashboards that help humans can destroy signals for AI agents, metastable failures and bugs that need two causes at once, and the map's most speculative link, Duhem-Quine underdetermination from the philosophy of science. Companion to our 'Code Lies, Facts Don't' episodes, via an IntuiBloom knowledge graph.

title: Stop Reading the Code, Part 2: The Human's New Job
description: If engineers no longer understand the code, what is their job? Automation bias, the map's addition, explains Sridharan's failure modes: plausible first answers, reviews that only confirm, and repros that match symptoms but not signals. Then her proposals: designing verification checks before code exists, humans as policy setters rather than 'meat proxies', and counting human interventions per bug as the honest measure of an agent-native software factory.

title: What You Really Want Isn't Happiness, Part 1: Not Too Bored, Not Too Stressed
description: Steve Yegge called it a favorite essay of the past three years or so. Joshua Fost argues that happiness, freedom and justice are all shadows of one deeper value: adaptive complexity. We unpack what "complex" really means, why the interesting stuff lives at the edge of chaos, and how flow fits Fost's theory. Made from an IntuiBloom graph. Explore the IntuiBloom graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/CDOoJf1ePmR3C3kWmPtkQj_UPRIYtTvtU3w_F07ukY4=

title: What You Really Want Isn't Happiness, Part 2: Palaces, Pines, and Machines
description: A kind dictator's palace or a messy free life? Fost's theory meets Berlin, Hayek and Rawls, invasive species, a thousand-year-old bristlecone pine, and AI. Then the critics get their turn on measurement, the gap between "is" and "ought", and falsifiability. Made from an IntuiBloom graph. Explore the IntuiBloom graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/CDOoJf1ePmR3C3kWmPtkQj_UPRIYtTvtU3w_F07ukY4=

title: You Didn't Choose Your Computer. You Just Got Used to It
description: Tom Ballard got AirDrop working between a Linux laptop and an iPhone, then started asking what else had been accepted for no reason. We cover Omarchy and Familiar, sour grapes psychology, software built for an audience of one, the HyperCard lineage, and the catches: maintenance, unpaid open-source labor, choice overload, and interoperability law. Made from an IntuiBloom graph. Explore the IntuiBloom graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/1CYZUhBdYj42NuplTg0yfHlE3Yd-J0bHxqjJ-Q9ysKk=

title: Why You Can't Microwave a Good Idea: Inside Google Labs
description: Lenny Rachitsky's ten takeaways from Google Labs head Josh Woodward: ideas come from small obsessed teams, product-market fit shows in people's eyes, labs keep an "almost possible" list, and people need a high "unlearning rate". Plus the history the post leaves out, from Bell Labs to Xerox PARC. Made from an IntuiBloom graph. Explore the IntuiBloom graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/hQHf1C6k4dspIgXpAID_g-yvmWRjdiD2ARGMwZAmbUE=

title: Every Kubernetes Concept Is a Scar: Inside the One Hidden Loop
description: Akhilesh Mishra's thread argues that every Kubernetes feature exists because of a specific production failure, and that underneath them all sits one loop: watch the actual state, compare it with the desired state, reconcile. We go through the IntuiBloom graph from pods to controllers and talk about what that story explains well and what it skips. Explore the IntuiBloom graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/MqRCNLk_tHsIbY0IfqLYc8lY2SfSKIyLZIfy6EFSPwg=

title: Pixels Over Software: The Thesis, the Frontier, the Blind Spots
description: Rob Phillips resurfaced his essay with a sharp framing: software will eventually be generated on the fly, and pixels are all you need. We go through the IntuiBloom graph on the essay's thesis, where the frontier is, and the blind spots it leaves open. Explore the IntuiBloom graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/l0y1s8y-2quuLDLVuckEuJMyt7p8BESkfPKAEndohsM=

title: Friction Is the Point: Mapping Shawn Smucker's Please Use AI
description: Shawn Smucker's "Please Use AI" is a satirical prose poem that keeps telling you to use AI for a meal plan, a last camping trip, a wedding toast, your art, and finally your own funeral song. Then it drops the irony for a quiet scene with a sleeping daughter. We walk through the IntuiBloom graph's layers: the poem's ironic machinery, the AI practices it mocks, and the human counter-account it defends, from friendship as care and friction as meaning to griefbots and Ted Chiang's argument about AI art. Explore the IntuiBloom graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/ZOgUzu3cN1PivxvlS9CVGWU8ZkeDRF7saeGLqahWn_s=

title: AI's Real Money Is Buried Four Layers Below ChatGPT, Part 1
description: Anish Moonka argues AI isn't a chatbot but a five-layer stack: energy, chips, cloud, models and applications, with most of the money in the layers nobody talks about. Using the IntuiBloom graph, we cover the giant 2026 capex from Amazon, Microsoft, Google and Meta, OpenAI's growth alongside its cash burn, the circular "revenue flows up, capital flows down" loop, and the electricity analogy behind "Infrastructure Gravity". Explore the IntuiBloom graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/WjQULoHFtcQEQGii0CV2KwDoiMMO8-yS_d9cbFelC5A=

title: AI's Real Money Is Buried Four Layers Below ChatGPT, Part 2
description: We climb Anish Moonka's AI stack layer by layer: power-hungry data centres, chip bottlenecks at Nvidia, TSMC and ASML, debt-funded cloud buildouts, cash-burning model labs, and data moats at the app layer. Then the bubble debate, DeepSeek, and what the IntuiBloom graph adds: the Jevons paradox, water, heat and land constraints, and how a viral investing essay can shape the market it describes. Explore the IntuiBloom graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/WjQULoHFtcQEQGii0CV2KwDoiMMO8-yS_d9cbFelC5A=

title: Forget Fine-Tuning: Agents That Rewrite Their Own Scaffold, Part 1
description: A new paper proposes harness learning: a trained "proposer" model reads how an AI agent's run went and edits its harness, the code that decides what the model sees, which tools it uses and how answers flow, while the model's own weights stay frozen. Using the IntuiBloom graph, we unpack the proposer-solver loop, meta-learning over programs, harness edits as gradient steps, and the paper's formulas in plain words. Explore the IntuiBloom graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/X3lkfCRNMZd0swji3SiUM9WbQCtzzlQx1ek7tXjIl-U=

title: Forget Fine-Tuning: Agents That Rewrite Their Own Scaffold, Part 2
description: Does harness learning work? On 21 unseen Reasoning Gym puzzle families the average revision score rises from 0.32 to 0.62, and the 4B proposer beats its 35B teacher on average; a HotpotQA-trained proposer keeps improving on unseen multi-hop QA benchmarks over ten rounds. We cover what the learned harnesses look like, the paper's limits, and where the IntuiBloom graph goes further: reward hacking, compute cost, history, and continually learning agents. Explore the IntuiBloom graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/X3lkfCRNMZd0swji3SiUM9WbQCtzzlQx1ek7tXjIl-U=

title: Attention: One Trick, All of AI, Maybe All of Mind
description: Natalie Wolchover's Quanta column traces how a 2014 translation trick by intern Dzmitry Bahdanau, working with Kyunghyun Cho and Yoshua Bengio, became the transformer and today's large language models. Using the IntuiBloom graph, we explain the queries, keys and values behind attention through a single ambiguous "it", Llion Jones's argument that next-word prediction is "AI-complete", why human thought seems to reach beyond language, the efficiency gap Jones now sees, and how the word "attention" itself can mislead. Explore the IntuiBloom graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/5h9MFZU_uHNUYXozKXgY1mPcstLdNJ-i3Ds1En23Kvg=

title: Attention: One Trick, All of AI, Maybe All of Mind (Deep Dive)
description: A longer, slower walk through Natalie Wolchover's Quanta column on attention. How an intern's 2014 translation fix, working with Kyunghyun Cho and Yoshua Bengio, beat the one-suitcase bottleneck; what queries, keys and values actually compute, worked through one ambiguous "it"; how the transformer scaled it; Llion Jones's case that next-word prediction is "AI-complete" and his doubts about efficiency; and why Wolchover thinks human thought reaches beyond language. We flag what the IntuiBloom graph adds: the grounding objection, the many meanings of "attention", global workspace theory and more. Explore the IntuiBloom graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/5h9MFZU_uHNUYXozKXgY1mPcstLdNJ-i3Ds1En23Kvg=

title: Buoyancy: Why Some AI Products Rise With Every New Model
description: Rajiv Ayyangar's essay 'Buoyancy' asks why the same model release lifts some AI products and sinks others. We cover plumbing vs scaffolding, why every workaround is a short bet on model progress, prompt sediment, the 94% vs 91% classifier choice, the thin-wrapper objection and 'Sherlocking', the hull that keeps you from being dissolved, what it means for careers, the greed-or-dread test, and the footnote that tides also go out. We also flag what the IntuiBloom graph adds, including Taleb's antifragility. Explore the IntuiBloom graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/93LC_FB0dTmTAE2cEz7JP0feQLz6SEiu8lQj2v7S7mY=

title: 38 Lessons From 10 AI Products — And Half Expire in a Year
description: PostHog shipped ten AI products and published 38 lessons, ending with a warning that half will be wrong within a year. We work out which half to keep: build AI only for real jobs, why PostHog's agent interface beat its own AI assistant five to one, context as the moat, skills, agents that run code, reliability over capability, tracing, small evals, the $6.67 cost per run, customers rebuilding you, prompt injection, and interfaces built for review. We flag the connections the IntuiBloom graph adds as its own hypotheses. Explore the IntuiBloom graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/6fVf1-1Z_za93OoYmDjhfH1tBQMu3k2KAXHOL5-xX-s=

title: From Mic Check to Launch: Your Podcast, Step by Step
description: How do you actually start a podcast? Following an IntuiBloom graph on the topic, we walk the path from deciding who the show is for and what it promises, through format, publishing schedule and episode planning, to recording, gear, editing, hosting and RSS, and getting into listening apps. Then come promotion, what listener numbers can and can't tell you, and keeping a show going without burning out. A hypothetical bike-repair show serves as a running example. Explore the IntuiBloom graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/t8yM7qpA7ta_j064uhddvPC78gDcaqeig0OuKoMtN5w=

title: When AI Makes Output Free, Outcomes Are the Only Currency
description: AI can make features, tickets and code almost free, so what should teams count? We dig into the output-to-outcome operating model credited to Mik Kersten and the ideas behind it: "Project to Product", the Flow Framework and flow efficiency, and the DORA metrics. We also cover the AI productivity paradox, Goodhart's law and how to guard against it, and why funding decides whether outcome thinking survives. Near the end we explore the IntuiBloom graph's own speculative ideas: a verification bottleneck and a "digital twin" of the organization. Explore the IntuiBloom graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/vuQe_O_kPjNNHykIepvhUU4kgI6OtV9KOi7Hi-lJTus=

title: Beyond Faster: How AI Can Expand What You Dare to Do
description: Felix Rieseberg, who works on Claude, wrote a tutorial on being more ambitious with AI models. Following an IntuiBloom graph of the essay, we walk through its four kinds of ambition: speed, altitude (aiming at the outcome, like replacing a quarterly deck), depth (expert instruments, raw data, an outside judge) and range (assembling a cross-field crew, methods not costumes). We cover the data and tools these need, then the psychology of why we hold back: self-efficacy, hard goals, Dantzig's "homework", the four-minute mile and permission to fail. We also flag the graph's own note on human oversight. Explore the IntuiBloom graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/w83OCxfKX2rKBzDbRideuYNmseXTqgFFeh2ihIiIMHo=

title: When AI agents outrun the org chart, the bottleneck moves
description: When AI agents finish the backlog faster than a company can plan, where does the work get stuck? Mik Kersten's keynote "Output to Outcome: When Agents Outrun the Org Chart" argues the bottleneck moves from output to the operating model itself. We cover the theory of constraints, a pattern across technological revolutions, and the parable of Peerless Auto putting an electric motor on an old drive shaft. We also go through Kersten's figures: teams use only about 8% of delivery time, TUI Group cut idea-to-customer time from about 200 days to 15, and Cognition's Devin reportedly throws away far more code than it ships. Then the proposed fix (the outcome loop, the outcome tree, AI-native SAFe and human ownership of every outcome) and the strongest objections the IntuiBloom graph raises. Explore the IntuiBloom graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/pJLbU0rwtwdwRWtUW4yekxSRJY_hBBQ8u0cH2cizHLw=

title: Code Is Cheap, Attention Isn't: Inside Agentic Code Review
description: When AI agents write code faster than any human can read it, review becomes the bottleneck. This deep dive walks through a new pattern-language paper by Davis, Gill, Hendrickson, Jones, Ma, Shoup and Wickett (Enterprise Technology Leadership Journal, Fall 2026). It argues that human review survives because of trust, compliance and accountability, and should give way to a layered verification stack: cheap automated checks, review depth set by risk, and decision records you can audit. We cover nine patterns, from small incremental changes and context engineering to adversarial AI review and teams of specialist review agents. Then come three real deployments: Block's agent-written changes that nobody felt they owned, Cloudflare's 131,246 review runs averaging about 1.2 findings each, and DryRun Security's tenant-isolation lesson. We finish at the speculative edge, the "dark software factory," where humans become curators of knowledge rather than reviewers. Built from an IntuiBloom knowledge graph. Explore the IntuiBloom graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/-7fKowO77Pq1ki0O8bGTMLGlAlxzEBirlKneSD3KLGI=

title: The Hidden Order Inside Neural Networks
description: Are neural networks hopelessly tangled, or already clean? We dive into Nick Cammarata's Goodfire essay, which argues that neurons that seem to do several unrelated jobs often do one deeper thing. We cover the cat-and-car neuron that turned out to detect a V shape, new audits of language-model neurons, neurons as gates, the case for scaling ordinary investigation with automated scientists, and the essay's own speculative safety implications. Explore the interactive IntuiBloom knowledge graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/pnqc18bsHamJDPNWDQa6RJkI9D3LdA8U9rqGwNVTJ5c=

title: Output to Outcome, Ch 0: When AI Removes the Bottleneck: From Outputs to Outcomes
description: Episode 1 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026). Chapter 0, "Foundations," comes after the Preface, Prompt and Introduction and before Part I's three models: the Product Operating Model, the Outcome Loop and the Outcome Tree. Kersten argues that AI is making knowledge output nearly free, which moves the bottleneck from producing work to the organization itself. We cover the productivity paradox, the Theory of Constraints (and the car-plant paint shop), the earlier shift to software as a service, Carlota Perez's model of technological revolutions and her "golden age," the "three million Shakespeare plays" problem, and Kersten's account of Cognition's weekly outcome loop, where it throws away much of its code. We also cover the risk he warns about: AI's gains piling up in a few giants. Built from an IntuiBloom knowledge graph. Explore the IntuiBloom graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/I8l7ns_g5OdvCAV1MWTNSnFsGyeJuJEj5a3JcMzyHIU=

title: Neural Networks Are Already Clean: Inside the Interpretability Reversal
description: When a neuron seems to respond to unrelated things, is the network a tangled knot, or have we just not figured it out yet? We dig into Nick Cammarata's Goodfire essay 'Neural Networks Are Already Clean,' which argues superposition should be the last explanation, not the first. Along the way: the cat-and-car neuron that was really a V detector, layers squeezed from 480 neurons to 10 that got coarser instead of tangled, the Santa answer that lived on neurons' negative side, a neuron that tracks Colorado, attribution graphs up to trillion-parameter models, and the essay's speculative case for spotting deception hiding in plain sight. Explore the interactive IntuiBloom knowledge graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/xcecd2NLj5r5gMJRl2BoZrp0nFUiPWnufzKmfjJst2o=

title: Output to Outcome, Ch 1: AI Won't Fix Your Company If the Bottleneck Isn't Code
description: Episode 2 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026). Chapter 1, "Product Operating Model," opens Part I, "Outcome Management," and is the first of the book's three foundational models, before the Outcome Loop (Ch 2) and the Outcome Tree (Ch 3). Kersten argues that AI's tenfold boost to coding won't help companies whose bottleneck sits elsewhere. In his State of the Industry data, only 8% of the time from idea to running software went to building it. We cover the Theory of Constraints and the jammed on-ramp, the history from McCallum's org chart to Gantt charts, Snowden's Cynefin framework and when to run a project versus a product, irreducible uncertainty and where AI can augment but not replace decisions, Reinertsen's life cycle profitability, the operating-model dysfunctions in Kersten's reports, and Commonwealth Bank of Australia's path from project to product to AI-native engineering. Discussion questions: 1) Is your team organized around projects that end, or products that keep going? What would change if it were the other way around? 2) Where is your on-ramp? Name the step between an idea and a customer that slows everything down, even when the coding is fast. 3) If your team had ten times more AI capacity next month, what work would it speed up that probably shouldn't be done at all? Built from an IntuiBloom knowledge graph. Explore the IntuiBloom graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/AL1vJA_m_BgKI2qgGiDOYX0qCm-QLrCkQtXXUnDLVzY=

title: From AI Skeptic to Agent Whisperer: Rethinking the Work
description: Mitchell Hashimoto's essay "My AI Adoption Journey" traces a measured path from AI skeptic to working with an agent alongside them most days. We cover Mitchell's three phases of adopting any tool (inefficiency, adequacy, discovery) and their six steps: dropping the chatbot for tool-using agents, doing the work twice to learn what agents do well, end-of-day agents for a "warm start," outsourcing the slam dunks with notifications off, "harness engineering" with AGENTS.md and verification tools, and always having an agent running. We also cover the open question Mitchell raises about skill formation, especially for juniors. Built from an IntuiBloom knowledge graph. Explore the IntuiBloom graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/cL0rFE_6eRziao0xBfGuG4A1e_jkUGwdg9V0AO7-u3Q=

title: Output to Outcome, Ch 2: The Outcome Loop: Constraints, AI Surplus, and the Next Bottleneck
description: Episode 3 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026). Chapter 2, "The Outcome Loop," sits in the middle of Part I, "Outcome Management." It builds on Chapter 1's Product Operating Model, sets up Chapter 3's Outcome Tree, and is the core model that the book's seven shifts in Part II build on. Kersten defines the loop as the feedback system that connects inputs (strategy and budget) to outputs (activities and artifacts) to outcomes (employee, customer and business) and back again. We cover production elasticity and Amazon, the lineage from outcome-based healthcare and Jobs to Be Done to OKRs, Kersten's own path from PhD research to Tasktop, key results versus KPIs, the TeenWellness worked example, why the loop is a hypothesis test, broken telemetry and the "counting procedures" trap, applying the Theory of Constraints, and how the VS Code team's bottleneck moved from delivery to onboarding to code review as AI took over more of the output. Discussion questions: 1) What is your team's version of counting procedures instead of tracking patients? 2) Pick one recent feature and trace it around the loop, from the strategy and budget behind it, to what was built, to what changed for customers. Where does the loop break? 3) Where's the bottleneck in your team right now? And if AI removed it, where do you think it would move next? Built from an IntuiBloom knowledge graph. title: Output to Outcome, Ch 3: The Outcome Tree: Scaling AI-Era Orgs Like Redwoods, Not Waterfalls
description: Episode 4 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026). Chapter 3, "The Outcome Tree," is the last of Part I's three foundational models, after the Product Operating Model and the Outcome Loop. We also cover the short Conclusion to Part I, which previews the book's seven shifts. Kersten's question is how to scale one Outcome Loop to hundreds or thousands of value streams. We cover the "AI in Waterfall" dysfunction, the coordination math (n times n minus one connections), matrix overlays, Kotter's "second operating system," Holacracy and Haier's RenDanHeYi, and Geoffrey West's sublinear and superlinear scaling. We also cover the nature behind the model: redwoods, fractals, insulin and abscisic acid. Then the tree itself, with value streams as leaves, MECE partitioning, objective and budget cascades, and branching factors. Finally, Kersten's own path from Xerox PARC and AspectJ to building the Outcome Tree at Tasktop with help from Adrian Cockcroft and the Reverse Conway Maneuver, and his speculative idea of "organization as code." Discussion questions: 1) Sketch your part of the organization as a tree. Does every team hang from one clear branch, or do some hang from several? 2) How many people do you need to involve to make an ordinary decision on your team? What would it take to cut that number in half? 3) If some of the leaves in your tree became AI agents, what would you want each of them to be allowed to touch? Built from an IntuiBloom knowledge graph. Explore the IntuiBloom graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/wy1k6uei1RLPRhr6g-_05H8FMtpccLiN6Qim_obVF64=

title: Building AI Native: Rethink Everything: When Agents Write the Code, Every Rule Breaks
description: A pilot of Building AI Native, a builder-to-builder show for engineers making AI-native products. We dig into Avi Flombaum's essay series "Rethink Everything": the claim that most software best practices were optimizations for a human programmer who no longer writes the code. We cover verification over line-by-line reading, one-shot rewrites against end-to-end tests, choosing languages by strength rather than familiarity, small services in one repository with deliberate duplication, owning your infrastructure, and types as agent feedback. Then the tradeoffs: comprehension debt, slow end-to-end suites and the identity question. We close with one experiment to try this week. Built from an IntuiBloom knowledge graph. Explore the IntuiBloom graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/15WWkavPUTJOECMY8Pg01uLzrIn4-skDE8s39LoSFdw=

title: Output to Outcome, Ch 4: From Silos to Value Streams: How AI Rewires the Org Chart
description: Episode 5 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026). Chapter 4 opens Part II, "The Seven Shifts," with the first shift: Functions to Flow. After Part I's three models (the Product Operating Model, the Outcome Loop and the Outcome Tree), Kersten argues that organizing around functional silos stops working when AI extends everyone's reach across domains. We cover handoffs and wait states, Priceline's drop from fifteen handoffs to five, and the Dedicated Leadership Model, Amazon's Single-Threaded Owners and Leaders, and single-, dual- and triple-leader structures. We also cover Kersten's claim that AI makes single leaders viable in more cases. Then value stream scope and "independence of action," SLAs for supporting functions, Value Stream Management and its lean manufacturing roots, capacity-based funding, and Weighted Shortest Job First. Finally, the TUI Group case: flow time cut from two hundred days to fifteen, a four-level AI literacy ladder, more than three thousand internal agents, and managers moving from owning people to owning outcomes. Discussion questions: 1) How many handoffs does a typical piece of work go through on your team before it reaches a customer? 2) What is the longest wait state in your process right now? And who has the power to remove it? 3) Does your value stream have one leader, or one matched pair, whose only job is its outcomes? If not, who owns it in practice? Built from an IntuiBloom knowledge graph. Explore the IntuiBloom graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/nc29idOXdpMrXAzgs_Q56M_LRVAkmU6S3QIsjww2o8w=

title: Output to Outcome, Ch 5: AI Made Output Cheap. Now Only Outcomes Matter
description: Episode 6 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026). Chapter 5, "Slop to Substance," is the second of Part II's seven shifts, after Chapter 4's move from functions to flow. Kersten argues that when AI makes output nearly unlimited, output metrics turn into vanity metrics, and only outcomes tell you whether work matters. We cover local optimization, Outcome Loop telemetry, and Strategic Portfolio Management. Then Plan Distribution (planned, unplanned, canceled and aged work, with only 25% of studied work aligned to strategy) and Goodhart's Law. Then the four Flow Items (features, defects, risks and debts), Flow Distribution, feature factories and the tech debt death spiral. Then the Flow Metrics Model: flow time, velocity, load and efficiency, and why not to use it on individuals. We also cover capacity planning from historical velocity, outcome metrics and attribution, Theory of Constraints, improvement objectives paired with employee happiness, agents that inspect Outcome Loops, and Vanguard's "Ideation Cliff." Discussion questions: 1) Which number on your team's dashboard would go up a hundredfold if agents did the work, without telling you anything useful? 2) Roughly what share of your team's work last quarter was planned, how much was unplanned, and how much was quietly abandoned? 3) If you could add one outcome metric to every review, what would it be? And could your team see its own contribution to it? Built from an IntuiBloom knowledge graph. Explore the IntuiBloom graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/DuZBgo8ax_G7-V03BxgwknLgZkgleMMO1_rduSuutK8=

title: Output to Outcome, Ch 6: One Cadence to Rule Them All: AI's Real Operating System
description: Episode 7 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026). Chapter 6, "Chaos to Cadence," is the third of Part II's seven shifts, after Functions to Flow and Slop to Substance. Kersten asks why billion-dollar Agile and AI transformations can leave companies feeling slower. His answers: missing outcome measurement, and Agile layered onto legacy planning as a "second operating system." We cover the tree whose leaves photosynthesize faster than its trunk can carry, coordination cost, and the Unified Cadence Model of shared annual, quarterly, monthly and weekly cycles. We also cover planning against fixed historical capacity, roadmap autonomy with visible dependencies, and the recursive planning cascade down the Outcome Tree. Then the inputs, outputs and outcomes value stream report (including AI token spend), calendar-aligned planning, and the merger of Planview's and Tasktop's cadences, where moving to one cadence cut meeting and reporting overhead in half. Discussion questions: 1) How many separate planning and review rhythms does your organization run? Which meetings exist mainly to translate between them? 2) When did you last find out about a change in plans weeks too late? What would have let you hear about it sooner? 3) Does your main business review actually make prioritization decisions, or does it mostly report status? Built from an IntuiBloom knowledge graph. Explore the IntuiBloom graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/tq1BMsbEJ7jb2yIKSe5k5O4Uyv6bsxfOf8skMCtOSMk=

title: Output to Outcome, Ch 7: From Messy Matrix to Modularity: Wiring Your Org for the Age of AI
description: Episode 8 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026). Chapter 7, "Matrix to Modularity," is the fourth of Part II's seven shifts, after Functions to Flow, Slop to Substance and Chaos to Cadence. Kersten argues that matrix and "dotted line" reporting creates a messy matrix of slow decisions, and that the fix is modular value streams built for independence of action. We cover high cohesion and low coupling (with LEGO, Linux and Google's overlapping messaging apps), Conway's Law and sociotechnical congruence, and the embed-versus-depend tradeoff. We also cover why improvement work belongs on the common parent's roadmap, one complexity domain per team, and Carliss Baldwin's option value. Then agents owning whole value streams, parallel hypothesis testing, John Lewis Partnership cutting delivery from ten days to 1.3, and Priceline's "Operating Model testing" taking complex flows from fifteen handoffs to five. Discussion questions: 1) How many people do you answer to, formally or informally? Which decisions slow down because of it? 2) Think of a dependency your team copied or worked around to move faster. Who owns cleaning it up, and is it on anyone's roadmap? 3) Is your team focused on one complexity domain, or spread across several? If you could hand one off, which would it be? Built from an IntuiBloom knowledge graph. Explore the IntuiBloom graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/sf8kMZeSghlFHdWwLvWwObHdgc8YlF8GliIW3LG2hnk=

title: Output to Outcome, Ch 8: Who Owns the Outcome? The Hidden Cost of Shared Accountability
description: Episode 9 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026). Chapter 8, "Objectives to Ownership," is the fifth of Part II's seven shifts, after Functions to Flow, Slop to Substance, Chaos to Cadence and Matrix to Modularity. Kersten argues that ownership is the main control mechanism of the Outcome Tree, and that functional, matrix and shared ownership all diffuse accountability. We cover the Outcome Ownership Model, matching leaders' incentives one to one with their value stream's objectives, and turning priority order into incentive weights. We also cover why shared objectives are a trap (with Google's named owners and Apple's directly responsible individuals), aligning title levels to the tree, and title imbalance in dual-leader pairs. Then technical program managers and AI for dependency scenarios, the five-by-five limit on objectives and key results, and 70% stretch goals. Finally, Kersten's post-ChatGPT reorganization at Planview into a three-in-the-box AI value stream, and the later move, like GitHub Copilot's, to spread AI engineers into product teams. Discussion questions: 1) Do the incentives of the people leading your work match the objectives they're asked to deliver? Where do they pull apart? 2) Name one objective in your organization that has more than one owner. What would change if one person, or one matched pair, owned it? 3) Is there a key result your team set low to be safe? What would you aim for if seventy percent counted as success? Built from an IntuiBloom knowledge graph. Explore the IntuiBloom graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/gKmd9RX8kLS-DUGpfbJV2ektCWKeh4MOoiv3FLTOfK4=

title: Output to Outcome, Ch 9: Different Rules for Different Bets: Managing the Core, Platforms and AI Incubation
description: Episode 10 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026). Chapter 9, "Divisions to Domains," is the sixth of Part II's seven shifts, after Functions to Flow, Slop to Substance, Chaos to Cadence, Matrix to Modularity and Objectives to Ownership. Kersten argues that one uniform Outcome Tree cannot manage both the existing business and disruptive AI bets, and that platform under-investment and stalled innovation share one root cause: no mechanism for segmenting value streams. We cover the Outcome Domain Model's four domains (core, platform, incubation and transformation), its roots in the Three Horizons Framework and Geoffrey Moore's Zone Management, Reinertsen's life cycle profitability, and the 10% revenue threshold for moving a product between domains. We also cover the illustrative budget, cadence, planned-work, Flow Distribution and flow time targets for each domain, the Cynefin mapping, splitting the core into growth, maintenance and sunset, managing cloud and AI token costs through the platform domain, and the leaders each domain needs. Finally, Kersten's Tasktop Viz pivot, from a 20% revenue shortfall to the company's top product. Discussion questions: 1) Which domain does most of your team's work belong to: core, platform, incubation, or transformation? And is it being measured that way? 2) Is there an experiment in your organization that's being judged by the same metrics as a mature product? What would a fair metric for it look like? 3) Which outside costs, like cloud hosting or AI tokens, does your team spend without anyone seeing them in the budget? Built from an IntuiBloom knowledge graph. Explore the IntuiBloom graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/BJUfe-XAJBasuIJRC7QRZiSrxWOFuPiKsJPuQ8RBgbs=

title: Output to Outcome, Ch 10: When Agents Do the Making: The Rise of the Outcome Manager
description: Episode 11 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026), and the finale of the main chapters. Chapter 10, "Managers to Makers," is the seventh and final shift, and this episode also covers the book's Conclusion. Kersten argues that the divide between makers and managers dissolves as AI takes over much of both making and coordination. We cover the maker's and manager's schedules, the Outcome Architecture Model, the historical pattern of makers who became great managers, the Outcome Loop of one and why AI "commoditizes intelligence but not intentionality," autonomous value streams and outcome managers, execution versus operational autonomy, and the Jevons paradox. We also cover the Outcome Tree as a control structure for agents (with Bostrom's paperclip problem), the "humans report to humans" rule, systems thinking, one-pizza teams, and Kersten's own path from developer to CEO. Then the Conclusion: learning to learn, shared intentionality, Samuel Butler's "Darwin Among the Machines," and a recap of all seven shifts, plus our look back at the series. A bonus episode on the book's Appendix, the Playbook, follows. Discussion questions: 1) Which parts of your week are maker time, and which are manager time? If AI took over your reporting and status work, what would you do with those hours? 2) Is there a piece of your team's work that could run as an autonomous value stream? And who would answer for it if it went wrong? 3) Which part of the Outcome Loop is outside your comfort zone: strategy, building, or measuring outcomes? What's one way you could stretch into it? Built from an IntuiBloom knowledge graph. Explore the IntuiBloom graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/WupMNV3aTIY5MNq0PAzh9CN8akNTY7nfX_g8WtDSYK4=

title: Output to Outcome, Bonus: The Playbook: Three Models and Seven Shifts in Practice
description: Episode 12 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026): a bonus, practical episode after the series finale. The book's Appendix, "Playbook," compresses the whole book into one implementation checklist. We walk through its problem, solution and target state, the three foundational models (the Product Operating Model, the Outcome Loop and the Outcome Tree) and all seven shifts, each with a reminder from its chapter and a small first step you could try (our suggestions, not the book's). We also run the playbook backwards from the dysfunctions Kersten names in each chapter, follow the TeenWellness example through the whole book, discuss pressure points raised by the IntuiBloom graph (Goodhart's Law, Conway's Law and the ambidextrous organization), and look back at the whole series. Discussion questions: 1) If you could start only one of the seven shifts next month, which would it be, and why that one? 2) Which item on the playbook would your organization find hardest to adopt? And what's really standing in the way? 3) Looking back across the whole book, which idea changed how you see your own work the most? Built from an IntuiBloom knowledge graph. title: Smarter Models, Sharper Apps: The Applied AI Specialization Bet
description: As foundation models get smarter, do AI products converge or specialize? We dig into a this-week exchange between @signulll, who argues that smarter models mean founders build in less intelligence and mostly add near-universal guardrails and direction (hence lots of look-alike products), and Box CEO Aaron Levie, who argues the opposite: the "wrapper" era was a symptom of weak models, and agents using tools, tasks that run for hours or days, agent swarms, domain-specific data and routing, and real workflow change management make domain-by-domain differentiation go up, except close to the labs' core use cases. We cover Rich Sutton's "The Bitter Lesson," RAG and wrappers, long-horizon autonomy and orchestration, a steelman of the convergence case, and whether the two really disagree. We also cover the graph's broader lenses: enterprise diffusion, trust and verification as a possible moat, Coase and Williamson on transaction costs and build versus buy, and where value is captured in the AI stack. Built from an IntuiBloom knowledge graph. Explore the IntuiBloom graph: https://www.IntuiBloom.com/share/ym6BeeBlz4LD-t7N4ocRoYDn3GQGlAtmiHKpIoLCwcI=

title: Black October: AI’s Cybershock—or a Warning Without Proof?
description: A self-described tech optimist says the vibes have shifted. In this deep dive on John Milinovich's X post "Black October" (October 22, 2026), we walk through the author's claims: a two-day wave of record-breaking cyberattacks, frontier AI coding agents that can be spun up by the thousands, nearly-as-capable open-weight models, and a "fast takeoff" with breakthroughs across science, then their practical advice (two-factor authentication, a password manager, identity protection, a separate network for smart devices) and the surprising call to start using AI. We present the claims as the author's, flag what the post doesn't source, and separate what you can check from what's interpretation. Built from an IntuiBloom knowledge graph.
